adjudication_label: Modeling assumptions and mass-loss correlations in oxidation
canonical_question: How do modeling assumptions regarding diffusion-controlled oxidation kinetics and observed microstructural depletion depths correlate with macroscopic mass loss data across different high-temperature regimes (850–1050 °C vs. 450 °C in molten salt)?

question_variants.question: Does the linear regression model used for the Arrhenius plot assume the oxidation mechanism remains strictly diffusion-controlled across the entire 850–1050 °C range?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text confirms that for the diffusion-controlled phenomenon studied, a linear regression model was fitted using Arrhenius curves, implying the assumption of a diffusion-controlled mechanism across the tested range.

answers.answer: The text states 'In a diffusion controlled phenomenon, a linear regression model was fitted using Arrhenius curves,' indicating the model assumes a diffusion-controlled mechanism.
evidence_spans: The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration.

Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure.
Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h.

source_evidence_spans: In a diffusion controlled phenomenon, a linear regression model was fitted using Arrhenius curves.

question_variants.question: How do the reported Cr depletion depths (~30 μm vs ~200 μm at 450 °C) correlate with the measured mass loss data for the two alloys?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The paper reports Cr depletion depths for AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (~30 μm) and DS2205 (~200 μm) at 450 °C and separately reports mass loss data showing DS2205 has significantly higher corrosion rates (~8-20 mm/year) than AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (~1-9 mm/year). While the trends correlate (greater depletion correlates with greater mass loss), the paper does not explicitly state a direct mathematical correlation or causal link between the specific depletion depths and the measured mass loss values, nor does it explain if the mass loss is solely due to Cr depletion depth.

answers.answer: The paper notes that at 450 °C, the Cr depletion depth in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 was ~30 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~200 μm. Separately, DS2205 showed greater mass loss (higher corrosion rate) compared to AlCoCrFeNi 2.1. The document does not explicitly correlate these specific numerical values.
answers.measurement_outcome: Cr depletion ~30 μm vs ~200 μm; Corrosion rate ~1 mm/year vs ~8 mm/year
answers.mechanism: Selective dissolution attributed to micro-galvanic coupling and phase stability
evidence_spans: Here, the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNI 2.1 EHEA in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt was investigated at 450 °C and 650 °C.
The performance of EHEA was compared with one of the benchmark dual-phase structural alloys, namely duplex steel 2205 (DS2205).
To explain the effect of eutectic microstructure on the local electrochemical activity, Scanning Kelvin Probe (SKP) analysis was utilized to measure the relative electron work function

cross_paper_synthesis.consensus: Both papers utilize AlCoCrFeNi-based high entropy alloys and observe significant material degradation at elevated temperatures, linking the phenomenon to chromium transport and depletion.
cross_paper_synthesis.different_approaches: The first paper (PMC9026100) employs a macroscopic kinetic modeling approach, fitting Arrhenius curves under the explicit assumption that the oxidation mechanism is diffusion-controlled across a solid-gas interface [2cabb99087f63967]. In contrast, the second paper (PMC9955357) adopts a microstructural and electrochemical approach, measuring specific chromium depletion depths in a molten salt environment and attributing the mechanism to selective dissolution and micro-galvanic coupling [9d27453f04a87991].
cross_paper_synthesis.condition_dependencies: The validity of the diffusion-controlled assumption is explicitly tied to the 850–1050 °C solid-gas regime [2cabb99087f63967]. The correlation between depletion depth and mass loss is specific to the 450 °C molten salt environment, where the Cr depletion depth (~30 μm vs. ~200 μm) is measured but not numerically correlated to the mass loss data (~1 mm/year vs. ~8 mm/year) in the provided text [9d27453f04a87991].
cross_paper_synthesis.contradictions: There are no direct contradictions; however, the papers address different regimes. The first assumes strict diffusion control, while the second identifies micro-galvanic coupling as a driver in a salt melt, suggesting that the 'diffusion-controlled' model may not fully capture the corrosion physics in the molten salt regime or at lower temperatures.
cross_paper_synthesis.evidence_strength: The diffusion control assumption is cited as a modeling premise within the text of the first paper [2cabb99087f63967]. The depletion and mass loss values in the second paper are presented as observed data points without an explicit mathematical correlation provided in the text [9d27453f04a87991].
cross_paper_synthesis.unresolved_gap: It remains unresolved whether the linear regression model based on diffusion control (PMC9026100) is applicable to the 450 °C molten salt regime where micro-galvanic effects are prominent (PMC9955357), nor is there an explicit functional link established between the magnitude of Cr depletion depth and the rate of mass loss in the molten salt study.
cross_paper_synthesis.candidate_hypothesis: The oxidation/corrosion mechanism in AlCoCrFeNi alloys transitions from a strictly diffusion-controlled regime at high temperatures (850–1050 °C) to a regime governed by localized electrochemical effects (micro-galvanic coupling) in molten salts at lower temperatures (450 °C), potentially invalidating the high-temperature diffusion model in the latter case.
cross_paper_synthesis.discriminating_experiment: Conduct an oxidation test on the same AlCoCrFeNi alloy in the 850–1050 °C range within a molten salt environment to determine if the Arrhenius kinetics remain linear and diffusion-controlled, or if the activation energy shifts due to micro-galvanic dominance observed at 450 °C.
